items.stem: You are writing a formal letter to someone whose name you do not know. Which sign-off is correct?
options: Love from
Yours faithfully
Yours sincerely
See you soon
items.answer: Yours faithfully
items.markingKey: ‘Dear Sir or Madam … Yours faithfully’; ‘Dear Mr X … Yours sincerely’.

items.stem: Task: Imagine you are a character writing a private journal entry about a frightening night. A student begins: ‘Report on the Night Crossing. Findings: the ferry was late.’ Explain what is wrong with this opening and suggest a better one.
items.answer: It uses report conventions; a journal should be personal and reflective. Better: ‘I am writing this on the quayside with salt still in my hair. Last night I really thought I had made a mistake.’
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: identifies the problem of form/register/voice; 1 mark: improved opening that suits the role and audience.

items.stem: Task: Imagine you are a business owner writing to the town council. A student begins: ‘The plan is rubbish and everyone knows it.’ Explain what is wrong with this opening and suggest a better one.
items.answer: It is rude, vague and unsupported; a formal letter needs a polite, reasoned opening. Better: ‘Dear Councillors, I respect the result of Saturday’s vote, but I must explain what it will mean for shops like mine.’
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: identifies the problem of form/register/voice; 1 mark: improved opening that suits the role and audience.

items.stem: Task: “Imagine you are the council’s parks officer. You write a reply to Dr Tanaka’s letter for the newspaper.” These sentences come from the letter to a newspaper ‘Protect Our Night Sky’: “I understand why many readers welcomed them; nobody wants to walk through a dark park feeling unsafe. … The floodlights now stay on until 2 a.m., seven nights a week, even though the park closes at ten.” Explain how you would use each detail in your response, developing it from the point of view of the council’s parks officer.
items.answer: Safety concerns: residents asked for lighting after incidents in the park. The late switch-off: admit the timing could be reviewed.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per detail identified and 1 mark per detail developed in role (max 4): safety concerns → residents asked for lighting after incidents in the park; the late switch-off → admit the timing could be reviewed.

items.stem: Task: “Imagine you are the director of the Museum of the Sea. You write a letter replying to the review.” These sentences come from the review ‘Review: The Floating Museum’: “The lower deck is the star attraction: a dimly lit gallery where a full-size whale skeleton hangs above visitors’ heads, slowly revolving as if still swimming. … The interactive navigation room, where you can steer a virtual ship through a storm, is equally gripping, although the queue on the Saturday I visited lasted forty minutes. Less successful is the upper deck, which is crammed with glass cases of maps and instruments labelled in tiny print.” Explain how you would use each detail in your response, developing it from the point of view of the director of the Museum of the Sea.
items.answer: Praise for the lower deck: pride in the whale gallery. Queues: timed tickets to reduce waiting. The upper deck: redesign with larger labels and interactive screens.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per detail identified and 1 mark per detail developed in role (max 6): praise for the lower deck → pride in the whale gallery; queues → timed tickets to reduce waiting; the upper deck → redesign with larger labels and interactive screens.

items.stem: Task: “Imagine you are Felix Mendes. You write a letter to the town council about the plan.” These sentences come from the news article ‘Town Votes to Close Main Street to Cars’: “‘Our children will breathe cleaner air, and our cafés will finally have room for outdoor tables,’ said councillor Ana Ribeiro. … Shop owner Felix Mendes, whose hardware store has traded on the street for thirty years, fears customers will simply drive to the out-of-town retail park instead. … The council has promised to build a 300-space car park on the edge of the centre and to review the scheme after one year.” Explain how you would use each detail in your response, developing it from the point of view of Felix Mendes.
items.answer: The councillor’s claim about cleaner air: accept the benefit but question the cost to businesses. Fear of losing customers to the retail park: shops in the centre may close. The promised car park: demand that it is built before April and close to shops.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per detail identified and 1 mark per detail developed in role (max 6): the councillor’s claim about cleaner air → accept the benefit but question the cost to businesses; fear of losing customers to the retail park → shops in the centre may close; the promised car park → demand that it is built before April and close to shops.

items.stem: Read the short story ‘The Power Cut’: “The lights died at 7.14, halfway through dinner. For a moment nobody moved. Then my little sister laughed, a high nervous sound, and Dad’s chair scraped back as he went to find the torch he swore was in the drawer by the sink. It was not. Outside, the whole street had vanished; even the streetlamps were blind. I had never seen our neighbourhood so dark. Without the hum of the fridge and the murmur of the television, the house seemed to hold its breath. We found three candles in the end, stubby and half-melted from someone’s birthday cake, and set them in a saucer in the middle of the table. In their wobbling light my parents’ faces looked younger, softer. Mum told a story about a storm in her village when she was a girl, a story I had never heard before. Nobody reached for a phone. When the power returned at 9.02, flooding the room with harsh white light, I was almost disappointed.” Imagine you are Mum. Later that night you write a diary entry about the power cut. In your journal, you should write about: what happened when the lights went out; what the evening by candlelight was like; your thoughts about family life. Base your answer on what you have read, but be careful to use your own words. Write about 250–300 words.
items.answer: Model opening: What an evening. At quarter past seven the lights went, and for two hours we were a family from my mother’s time: four faces round three stubby candles… The response then develops: Dad searching for the torch (affectionate amusement at his confidence); the birthday-cake candles (making do; memories of the birthday); telling the storm story (surprise that her children had never heard it; memories of childhood); no phones (wish for more evenings like this).
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10 (extended response in role (journal)): Reading 5 marks, Writing 5 marks. Reading – top band (5): ideas from the passage are thoroughly used, developed and extended with convincing inferences; all three bullets addressed; a consistent, convincing voice; middle band (3–4): relevant ideas with some development or selection; lower band (1–2): few relevant ideas, often lifted or repeated. Writing – top band (5): fluent, well organised, own words, register and form fully suited to the task; middle band (3–4): clear and mostly accurate, some own words; lower band (1–2): lifted phrases, weak organisation or frequent errors. Indicative content: Dad searching for the torch → affectionate amusement at his confidence. The birthday-cake candles → making do; memories of the birthday. Telling the storm story → surprise that her children had never heard it; memories of childhood. No phones → wish for more evenings like this. Form: a private, reflective first-person voice exploring thoughts and feelings; an honest, informal tone and references to the time of writing.

items.stem: Read the short story ‘The Last Mango Tree’: “Grandfather walked the orchard every evening, even after the land had been sold. He moved slowly between the rows, touching each trunk as if he were taking attendance at a school register. Most of the trees were already gone; the developers had cleared the eastern field in a single week, and now orange flags fluttered where the guavas had been. Only the old mango by the well remained. ‘Planted it the year your mother was born,’ he told me, though I had heard the story a hundred times. Its bark was cracked like a dry riverbed, and its lowest branch dipped so close to the ground that I could sit on it without jumping. That evening he did not speak for a long while. He pressed his palm flat against the trunk and kept it there. Then he took out his pocket knife, cut a single green mango and handed it to me. ‘Keep the stone,’ he said. ‘Plant it somewhere they can’t reach.’” Imagine you are the narrator, now an adult. You write a letter to your grandfather telling him what happened to the mango stone. In your letter, you should write about: your memories of the last evening in the orchard; what you understood about his feelings; what you did with the stone and why. Base your answer on what you have read, but be careful to use your own words. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model opening: Dear Grandfather, the stone you gave me that evening is now a tree taller than I am. I still remember the way you pressed your hand against the old mango, as if you were listening to it… The response then develops: Grandfather’s evening walk and touching the trees (you now understand he was saying goodbye to old friends); the cleared field and orange flags (anger or sadness at how quickly the land was destroyed); his silent hand on the trunk (his grief, which he could not express in words); his instruction about the stone (a promise kept: the stone planted somewhere safe as a living memorial).
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 12 (extended response in role (letter)): Reading 6 marks, Writing 6 marks. Reading – top band (5–6): ideas from the passage are thoroughly used, developed and extended with convincing inferences; all three bullets addressed; a consistent, convincing voice; middle band (3–4): relevant ideas with some development or selection; lower band (1–2): few relevant ideas, often lifted or repeated. Writing – top band (5–6): fluent, well organised, own words, register and form fully suited to the task; middle band (3–4): clear and mostly accurate, some own words; lower band (1–2): lifted phrases, weak organisation or frequent errors. Indicative content: Grandfather’s evening walk and touching the trees → you now understand he was saying goodbye to old friends. The cleared field and orange flags → anger or sadness at how quickly the land was destroyed. His silent hand on the trunk → his grief, which he could not express in words. His instruction about the stone → a promise kept: the stone planted somewhere safe as a living memorial. Form: an opening such as “Dear …” and a suitable sign-off; a clear purpose stated early and a register suited to the recipient.

items.stem: Which feature is most important in a speech written in role?
options: A dated heading
Subheadings
Footnotes
Direct address to the audience
items.answer: Direct address to the audience
items.markingKey: Speeches are spoken to listeners.

items.stem: In an extended response, what does it mean to ‘develop’ an idea from the passage?
options: To go beyond what is stated by inferring causes, feelings or consequences that fit the text
To repeat the idea several times
To invent events unconnected to the text
To copy the idea in the writer’s words
items.answer: To go beyond what is stated by inferring causes, feelings or consequences that fit the text
items.markingKey: Development = plausible extension grounded in the text.

items.stem: Task: “Imagine you are Mira. The morning after the crossing you write a journal entry.” A student’s response includes this sentence copied from the short story ‘The Night Ferry’: ‘A deckhand passed, whistling, and nodded at her as though night crossings were the most ordinary thing in the world.’ Explain why this only repeats the passage, and suggest how the student could develop the idea.
items.answer: It retells the text without interpreting it, so it shows little R3 development. Development: his ease could have reassured her, or made her feel more like an outsider.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: recognises repetition/lifting; 1 mark: plausible development (his ease could have reassured her, or made her feel more like an outsider); further mark for linking it to the role and purpose.

items.stem: Task: “Imagine you are one of the students being taught in shifts. You write a letter to the regional government.” A student’s response includes this sentence copied from the news article ‘Flood Recovery in the River District’: ‘However, the district’s only secondary school remains shut, and around 600 students are being taught in shifts at a primary school four kilometres away.’ Explain why this only repeats the passage, and suggest how the student could develop the idea.
items.answer: It retells the text without interpreting it, so it shows little R3 development. Development: less teaching time; exam worries.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: recognises repetition/lifting; 1 mark: plausible development (less teaching time; exam worries); further mark for linking it to the role and purpose.

items.stem: Writing as the council’s parks officer, develop this detail from the letter to a newspaper ‘Protect Our Night Sky’ into two or three sentences that infer thoughts, feelings or consequences: ‘I understand why many readers welcomed them; nobody wants to walk through a dark park feeling unsafe.’
items.answer: Detail: safety concerns. Developed in role: residents asked for lighting after incidents in the park.
items.markingKey: Mark points: credit plausible inference grounded in the detail, written in role; indicative: safety concerns → residents asked for lighting after incidents in the park. No credit for copying.

items.stem: Writing as a member of the eco-club, develop each of these details from the speech ‘Speech to the Youth Climate Forum’ into two or three sentences that infer thoughts, feelings or consequences: ‘So we raised money, we wrote to the council, and in November we planted twenty saplings.’ ‘In twenty years, a pupil you will never meet will sit in their shade and not even think about it.’
items.answer: Detail: the club’s fundraising. Developed in role: young people are willing to help; the council should match it. Detail: future pupils. Developed in role: planting now is an investment for the future.
items.markingKey: Mark points: credit plausible inference grounded in the detail, written in role; indicative: the club’s fundraising → young people are willing to help; the council should match it; future pupils → planting now is an investment for the future. No credit for copying.

items.stem: Writing as Mr Okafor, develop each of these details from the short story ‘First Day at the Workshop’ into two or three sentences that infer thoughts, feelings or consequences: ‘I swept for an hour.’ ‘I said nothing.’
items.answer: Detail: the hour of sweeping. Developed in role: a lesson that a craftsman respects the workshop before touching wood. Detail: the apprentice’s silence. Developed in role: a sign of patience and respect that impressed him.
items.markingKey: Mark points: credit plausible inference grounded in the detail, written in role; indicative: the hour of sweeping → a lesson that a craftsman respects the workshop before touching wood; the apprentice’s silence → a sign of patience and respect that impressed him. No credit for copying.

items.stem: Task based on the short story ‘The Last Mango Tree’: “Imagine you are the narrator, now an adult. You write a letter to your grandfather telling him what happened to the mango stone. In your letter, you should write about: your memories of the last evening in the orchard; what you understood about his feelings; what you did with the stone and why.” Relevant lines: “He moved slowly between the rows, touching each trunk as if he were taking attendance at a school register. Most of the trees were already gone; the developers had cleared the eastern field in a single week, and now orange flags fluttered where the guavas had been. … He pressed his palm flat against the trunk and kept it there. … ‘Keep the stone,’ he said.” (a) Identify two details from the lines that you could use in your response, and state which bullet point each would support. (b) Explain why developed ideas are rewarded more highly than repeated ones.
items.answer: (a) His silent hand on the trunk; the cleared field and orange flags (each linked to a suitable bullet). (b) R3 rewards developing and evaluating ideas; repetition only shows basic understanding (R1).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per relevant detail linked to a bullet [2] (b) link to R3 [2]

items.stem: Task based on the news article ‘Flood Recovery in the River District’: “Imagine you are one of the students being taught in shifts. You write a letter to the regional government. In your letter, you should write about: how the flood and school closure have affected you; what daily life is like now; what you want the government to decide and why.” Relevant lines: “The remaining families are still living with relatives or in temporary housing at the sports centre. … However, the district’s only secondary school remains shut, and around 600 students are being taught in shifts at a primary school four kilometres away. … Engineers have recommended raising the flood wall by one metre and restoring wetlands upstream to slow the water in future.” (a) For each detail, explain how you would develop it beyond what the text states. (b) Explain why developed ideas are rewarded more highly than repeated ones.
items.answer: (a) Long journeys, cost and tiredness; less teaching time; exam worries. (b) R3 rewards developing and evaluating ideas; repetition only shows basic understanding (R1).
items.markingKey: (a) 2 marks per developed, plausible extension [4] (b) link to R3 [2]

items.stem: Task: “Imagine you are the director of the Museum of the Sea. You write a letter replying to the review.” A student’s response includes this sentence copied from the review ‘Review: The Floating Museum’: ‘The interactive navigation room, where you can steer a virtual ship through a storm, is equally gripping, although the queue on the Saturday I visited lasted forty minutes.’ Explain why this only repeats the passage, and suggest how the student could develop the idea.
items.answer: It retells the text without interpreting it, so it shows little R3 development. Development: timed tickets to reduce waiting.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: recognises repetition/lifting; 1 mark: plausible development (timed tickets to reduce waiting); further mark for linking it to the role and purpose.

items.stem: What does ‘register’ mean?
options: The list of students in a class
The level of formality of language, chosen to suit the audience and purpose
The speed of reading
The number of paragraphs
items.answer: The level of formality of language, chosen to suit the audience and purpose
items.markingKey: Register = formality.

items.stem: A student writing for Year 10 students in an assembly wrote: ‘It is recommended that pupils reduce the quantity of discarded food.’ Rewrite it in an appropriate register and explain your choices.
items.answer: ‘So here’s my challenge to all of you: take only what you’ll actually eat.’ – direct address and a friendly challenge suit a peer audience.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: meaning kept in an appropriate informal register; 1 mark: explanation of a specific change (e.g. direct address and a friendly challenge suit a peer audience).

items.stem: Rewrite this sentence so that it suits your own private journal, and explain one change you made: ‘It is with regret that I report my failure to remain calm.’
items.answer: ‘I really lost my nerve today, and I hate admitting it.’ – honest, personal first-person voice.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: meaning kept in an appropriate informal register; 1 mark: explanation of a specific change (e.g. honest, personal first-person voice).

items.stem: Rewrite each sentence in a register suited to the audience named, keeping its meaning. Explain how the intended audience shaped the choices you made when rewriting.
items.answer: For a mountain hut warden: clear, factual account without exaggerated slang. For your own private journal: honest, personal first-person voice.
items.markingKey: specific choice of vocabulary or tone linked to the audience [2]

items.stem: Rewrite each sentence in a register suited to the audience named, keeping its meaning. (a) Rewrite ‘The canteen food is gross and the queues are mad long.’ for the Head of Year. (b) Explain how the intended audience shaped the choices you made when rewriting.
items.answer: (a) Many students are unhappy with the quality of the food and the length of the queues. (b) For the town council: polite modal ‘would ask’, precise vocabulary, no slang. For the Head of Year: measured, impersonal phrasing suitable for a staff reader.
items.markingKey: (a) appropriate formal register, meaning kept [2] (b) specific choice of vocabulary or tone linked to the audience [2]

items.stem: Based on the travel writing ‘Crossing the Salt Flats’, write the opening paragraph (about 100–150 words) of your response to this task: “Imagine you are Luis, the driver. You write an entry for a travel guidebook advising visitors to the salt flats. In your guide, you should write about: the best time of year to visit and why; what visitors will see and experience; how to stay safe and comfortable.” Then explain three choices you made to create an appropriate voice and register for Luis, the driver.
items.answer: Model opening: Visitors ask me every week: when should I come? My answer depends on what you want to see. Come in the rainy season and you will drive across the sky itself… Choices: practical advice organised clearly for visitors; second-person address and an informative, enthusiastic tone; vocabulary and viewpoint that reflect Luis, the driver.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10 (voice and register in a guide). Top band (8–10): a convincing, consistent voice for Luis, the driver; form and register fully suited; ideas from the passage woven in; three precise, well-explained choices. Middle band (5–7): appropriate voice and register for most of the paragraph; choices explained in general terms. Lower band (1–4): register insecure or inconsistent; explanations vague or missing. Indicative content: practical advice organised clearly for visitors; second-person address and an informative, enthusiastic tone; details such as the rainy-season mirror, the glare.

items.stem: Which is an opinion?
options: The museum deserves its crowds.
The museum is in a converted cargo ship.
The queue lasted forty minutes.
A sandwich and a juice cost eight euros.
items.answer: The museum deserves its crowds.
items.markingKey: A judgement that can be disagreed with.

items.stem: What is the writer’s attitude in the leaflet ‘Visiting the Coral Reef Responsibly’? Explain with reference to: ‘Help us keep it that way by following these simple guidelines.’
items.answer: The writer is friendly but firm; the writers care deeply about the reef. The words ‘Help us keep it that way’ show this (inclusive and friendly).
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: attitude (friendly but firm; the writers care deeply about the reef); 1 mark: explanation of how the quotation shows it (inclusive and friendly).

items.stem: What is the writer’s attitude in the autobiography ‘Learning to Swim at Forty’? Explain with reference to: ‘I sank like a dropped spanner.’
items.answer: The writer is self-mocking about past fears but warm and encouraging about learning as an adult. The words ‘I sank like a dropped spanner’ show this (humour at the writer’s own expense).
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: attitude (self-mocking about past fears but warm and encouraging about learning as an adult); 1 mark: explanation of how the quotation shows it (humour at the writer’s own expense).

items.stem: Read this extract from the travel writing ‘The Bus to Kathmandu’: “We arrived eleven hours later, stiff, dusty and somehow friends.” Explain how the writer uses a fact to support their viewpoint.
items.answer: We arrived eleven hours later gives verifiable support, making the writer’s view seem reasonable and evidence-based.
items.markingKey: fact linked to view [2]

items.stem: Re-read these sentences from the interview ‘The Mountain Rescue Volunteer’: “Sipho Ndlovu has been called out 212 times in eleven years with the Drakensberg mountain rescue team, and he still keeps his boots by the front door. … ‘We found them at dawn, cold and frightened but alive. I have never been so tired or so happy.’ Asked why he continues, he shrugs.” (a) Identify one opinion from the extract. (b) Explain how the writer uses a fact to support their viewpoint.
items.answer: (a) ‘I have never been so tired or so happy’ (b) Called out 212 times in eleven years gives verifiable support, making the writer’s view seem reasonable and evidence-based.
items.markingKey: (a) I have never been so tired or so happy (any judgement) [1] (b) fact linked to view [2]

items.stem: Read the report ‘Canteen Food Waste Report’: “Report to the Head of Year 10: Canteen Food Waste. Purpose: This report presents the findings of a two-week survey of food waste in the school canteen and recommends ways to reduce it. Findings: Students threw away an average of 41 kilograms of food each day. The largest single source of waste was rice, which accounted for almost a third of the total, followed by cooked vegetables. Waste was highest on Fridays, when a quarter of students said they skipped lunch to leave early for sports fixtures. In a questionnaire completed by 212 students, the most common reasons given for leaving food were that portions were too large (46 per cent) and that meals went cold while students queued (31 per cent). Recommendations: First, students should be able to choose a small or regular portion. Second, a second serving counter should be opened at peak times to shorten queues. Finally, uneaten food that is safe to use should be offered to the local food bank, with which the school already has links.” How convincingly does the writer present their views? In your answer, identify the main viewpoint and attitudes; evaluate how well they are supported by facts, examples and language; and reach your own reasoned judgement.
items.answer: Viewpoint: concerned but objective and practical. Support: facts such as Students threw away an average of 41 kilograms; Waste was highest on Fridays. Opinions: students should be able to choose a small or regular portion. Methods: ‘average of 41 kilograms’ – precise statistics show objectivity. ‘Recommendations:’ – focus on practical solutions. Judgement: e.g. largely convincing because claims are backed by specific details, though some statements are opinion rather than evidence.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10 (evaluating viewpoints (R3)). Top band (8–10): clear grasp of viewpoint and attitudes; evaluation distinguishes fact from opinion and judges the strength of evidence and the effect of language; a sustained, well-supported judgement. Middle band (5–7): identifies viewpoint and some methods with some evaluation; judgement partly supported. Lower band (1–4): mainly retells the content; little evaluation. Indicative content: concerned but objective and practical; facts: Students threw away an average of 41 kilograms; Waste was highest on Fridays; opinions: students should be able to choose a small or regular portion; ‘average of 41 kilograms’ – precise statistics show objectivity. ‘Recommendations:’ – focus on practical solutions.

items.stem: A journal entry written in role should mainly
options: reveal the character’s private thoughts and feelings
address a large audience
give instructions to visitors
list statistics under headings
items.answer: reveal the character’s private thoughts and feelings
items.markingKey: Journals are reflective and personal.

items.stem: Explain two features you should include when responding to this task based on the short story ‘The Power Cut’: “Imagine you are Mum. Later that night you write a diary entry about the power cut. In your journal, you should write about: what happened when the lights went out; what the evening by candlelight was like; your thoughts about family life.”
items.answer: A private, reflective first-person voice exploring thoughts and feelings; an honest, informal tone and references to the time of writing. The voice should be that of Mum, using details from the passage.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark per relevant, explained feature of a journal in role (e.g. a private, reflective first-person voice exploring thoughts and feelings); 1 mark for linking voice to Mum.

items.stem: Task: “Imagine you are a teacher who disagrees with the writer. You write an article for the same newspaper in reply.” These sentences come from the opinion article ‘Should Homework Be Banned?’: “What I object to is busywork: tasks set because a timetable says so, not because anyone will learn from them. Schools should set less homework, set it better and, above all, explain why it matters.” Explain how you would use each detail in your response, developing it from the point of view of a teacher who disagrees with the writer.
items.answer: Busywork: agree pointless tasks should go; defend practice and revision. Explaining purpose: teachers can explain; parents can support routines.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per detail identified and 1 mark per detail developed in role (max 4): busywork → agree pointless tasks should go; defend practice and revision; explaining purpose → teachers can explain; parents can support routines.

items.stem: Read the review ‘Review: The Floating Museum’: “Housed in a converted cargo ship moored in Lisbon’s harbour, the new Museum of the Sea promises ‘an unforgettable voyage through five centuries of ocean history’. For the most part, it delivers. The lower deck is the star attraction: a dimly lit gallery where a full-size whale skeleton hangs above visitors’ heads, slowly revolving as if still swimming. Children around me gasped; one small boy refused to leave. The interactive navigation room, where you can steer a virtual ship through a storm, is equally gripping, although the queue on the Saturday I visited lasted forty minutes. Less successful is the upper deck, which is crammed with glass cases of maps and instruments labelled in tiny print. After the drama below, it feels like reading a textbook in a cupboard. The café, meanwhile, is overpriced: eight euros for a sandwich and a juice. Overall, though, this is a bold, imaginative museum that deserves its crowds. Go early, go hungry for wonder — and bring your own lunch.” Imagine you are the director of the Museum of the Sea. You write a letter replying to the review. In your letter, you should write about: thanks for the praise; your response to the criticisms; changes you will make. Base your answer on what you have read, but be careful to use your own words. Write about 250–300 words.
items.answer: Model opening: Dear Editor, on behalf of everyone at the Museum of the Sea, thank you for your generous review. We were delighted that our whale made the children gasp… The response then develops: praise for the lower deck (pride in the whale gallery); queues (timed tickets to reduce waiting); the upper deck (redesign with larger labels and interactive screens); café prices (introduce a cheaper family menu).
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10 (extended response in role (letter)): Reading 5 marks, Writing 5 marks. Reading – top band (5): ideas from the passage are thoroughly used, developed and extended with convincing inferences; all three bullets addressed; a consistent, convincing voice; middle band (3–4): relevant ideas with some development or selection; lower band (1–2): few relevant ideas, often lifted or repeated. Writing – top band (5): fluent, well organised, own words, register and form fully suited to the task; middle band (3–4): clear and mostly accurate, some own words; lower band (1–2): lifted phrases, weak organisation or frequent errors. Indicative content: Praise for the lower deck → pride in the whale gallery. Queues → timed tickets to reduce waiting. The upper deck → redesign with larger labels and interactive screens. Café prices → introduce a cheaper family menu. Form: an opening such as “Dear …” and a suitable sign-off; a clear purpose stated early and a register suited to the recipient.

items.stem: Read the opinion article ‘Should Homework Be Banned?’: “Every evening, in millions of homes, the same battle is fought over the kitchen table. Parents nag, children sulk, and a worksheet on fractions somehow takes two hours. It is time we asked whether homework is worth the misery. The evidence is far less clear than many teachers assume. Research suggests that for primary pupils homework makes little difference to achievement, while for older students modest amounts — around an hour a night — can help. Beyond that, the benefits fall away and stress rises. Yet many teenagers report three or more hours a night, squeezed in between sport, chores and part-time jobs. I am not arguing for banning homework altogether. Reading for pleasure, practising a musical instrument or revising for a test are valuable habits. What I object to is busywork: tasks set because a timetable says so, not because anyone will learn from them. Schools should set less homework, set it better and, above all, explain why it matters. Our children’s evenings are not an extension of the school day.” Imagine you are a teacher who disagrees with the writer. You write an article for the same newspaper in reply. In your article, you should write about: which of the writer’s points you accept; which points you challenge and why; what good homework looks like. Base your answer on what you have read, but be careful to use your own words. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model opening: Last week your columnist described homework as a nightly battle. As a teacher of twenty years, I recognise the picture — but I do not accept the conclusion… The response then develops: research that modest homework helps (agree on quantity; argue for quality); the emotive picture of family conflict (challenge it as exaggerated); busywork (agree pointless tasks should go; defend practice and revision); explaining purpose (teachers can explain; parents can support routines).
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 12 (extended response in role (article)): Reading 6 marks, Writing 6 marks. Reading – top band (5–6): ideas from the passage are thoroughly used, developed and extended with convincing inferences; all three bullets addressed; a consistent, convincing voice; middle band (3–4): relevant ideas with some development or selection; lower band (1–2): few relevant ideas, often lifted or repeated. Writing – top band (5–6): fluent, well organised, own words, register and form fully suited to the task; middle band (3–4): clear and mostly accurate, some own words; lower band (1–2): lifted phrases, weak organisation or frequent errors. Indicative content: Research that modest homework helps → agree on quantity; argue for quality. The emotive picture of family conflict → challenge it as exaggerated. Busywork → agree pointless tasks should go; defend practice and revision. Explaining purpose → teachers can explain; parents can support routines. Form: a headline and an engaging opening paragraph; a lively but controlled voice suited to the publication’s readers.

items.stem: Task: “Imagine you are Mr Okafor. That evening you write a journal entry about your new apprentice’s first day.” Which is the best development of the detail about telling the apprentice they were late from the short story ‘First Day at the Workshop’?
options: ‘You’re late,’ he said.
Mention telling the apprentice they were late.
Fear and disorientation; perhaps set off too late.
A deliberate test of whether they would argue or accept discipline.
items.answer: A deliberate test of whether they would argue or accept discipline.
items.markingKey: A deliberate test of whether they would argue or accept discipline – it extends the detail with a plausible inference; the others only repeat the text or are unrelated.

items.stem: Task: “Imagine you are a teacher who disagrees with the writer. You write an article for the same newspaper in reply.” A student’s response includes this sentence copied from the opinion article ‘Should Homework Be Banned?’: ‘Research suggests that for primary pupils homework makes little difference to achievement, while for older students modest amounts — around an hour a night — can help.’ Explain why this only repeats the passage, and suggest how the student could develop the idea.
items.answer: It retells the text without interpreting it, so it shows little R3 development. Development: agree on quantity; argue for quality.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: recognises repetition/lifting; 1 mark: plausible development (agree on quantity; argue for quality); further mark for linking it to the role and purpose.

items.stem: Writing as a licensed snorkelling guide, develop this detail from the leaflet ‘Visiting the Coral Reef Responsibly’ into two or three sentences that infer thoughts, feelings or consequences: ‘Use reef-safe sun cream.’
items.answer: Detail: sun cream. Developed in role: sell approved brands on boats.
items.markingKey: Mark points: credit plausible inference grounded in the detail, written in role; indicative: sun cream → sell approved brands on boats. No credit for copying.

items.stem: Task based on the short story ‘The Night Ferry’: “Imagine you are Mira. The morning after the crossing you write a journal entry. In your journal, you should write about: what happened before and during the departure; your thoughts and feelings during the night; how you now feel about travelling alone.” Relevant lines: “The ferry left the harbour at nine, an hour late, because the captain refused to cast off until the last delivery van had rattled up the ramp. … Within minutes the lights of the town had shrunk to a smudge, and then the fog swallowed them completely. … She had told her mother she would be fine travelling alone; she had said it three times, as if repeating it would make it true. … A deckhand passed, whistling, and nodded at her as though night crossings were the most ordinary thing in the world.” (a) Identify two details from the lines that you could use in your response, and state which bullet point each would support. (b) Explain why developed ideas are rewarded more highly than repeated ones.
items.answer: (a) The calm deckhand; the town disappearing in the fog (each linked to a suitable bullet). (b) R3 rewards developing and evaluating ideas; repetition only shows basic understanding (R1).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per relevant detail linked to a bullet [2] (b) link to R3 [2]

items.stem: Rewrite this sentence so that it suits Year 10 students in an assembly, and explain one change you made: ‘It is recommended that pupils reduce the quantity of discarded food.’
items.answer: ‘So here’s my challenge to all of you: take only what you’ll actually eat.’ – direct address and a friendly challenge suit a peer audience.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: meaning kept in an appropriate informal register; 1 mark: explanation of a specific change (e.g. direct address and a friendly challenge suit a peer audience).

items.stem: Rewrite this sentence so that it suits a museum director, and explain one change you made: ‘Your café is a total rip-off.’
items.answer: ‘The café’s prices seem high for what is offered.’ – tactful, evaluative language.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: meaning kept in an appropriate formal register; 1 mark: explanation of a specific change (e.g. tactful, evaluative language).

items.stem: Rewrite each sentence in a register suited to the audience named, keeping its meaning. Rewrite ‘I am writing to inform you that the journey was extremely unpleasant.’ for a close friend, in a letter.
items.answer: You won’t believe the journey I’ve just had — it was awful!
items.markingKey: appropriate informal register, meaning kept [2]

items.stem: In the review ‘Review: The Floating Museum’, the writer writes: ‘Overall, though, this is a bold, imaginative museum that deserves its crowds.’ What does this reveal about the writer’s viewpoint?
items.answer: The writer is broadly enthusiastic, with honest reservations. The words ‘deserves its crowds’ show this (recommends it).
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: attitude (broadly enthusiastic, with honest reservations); 1 mark: explanation of how the quotation shows it (recommends it).

items.stem: Read this extract from the diary ‘Turtle Hatchery Diary’: “We marked each one with a numbered stake and logged the GPS position, as we have been taught. Nest 41 had been dug up by a dog during the night. … I hope I was telling the truth: the project’s funding ends in December, and nobody knows what happens after that.” Summarise the writer’s overall attitude, with a brief reference to the text.
items.answer: Dedicated and proud of the work, but anxious about the future: care and professionalism (‘as we have been taught’).
items.markingKey: attitude + evidence [2]

items.stem: Read this extract from the travel writing ‘The Bus to Kathmandu’: “It left at nine, after the driver had finished his tea, his second tea and a long conversation with a man selling oranges. … We arrived eleven hours later, stiff, dusty and somehow friends.” (a) Identify one opinion from the extract. (b) Explain how the writer uses a fact to support their viewpoint.
items.answer: (a) ‘somehow friends’ (b) We arrived eleven hours later gives verifiable support, making the writer’s view seem reasonable and evidence-based.
items.markingKey: (a) somehow friends (any judgement) [1] (b) fact linked to view [2]

items.stem: In Question 4, what does writing ‘in role’ mean?
options: Writing as a character or person from the passage, using their viewpoint and voice
Writing a story with new characters
Writing as yourself giving opinions about the passage
Writing a summary of the passage
items.answer: Writing as a character or person from the passage, using their viewpoint and voice
items.markingKey: You adopt the given persona.

items.stem: Task: Imagine you are a rescued teenager writing a letter of thanks to a rescue volunteer. A student begins: ‘To whom it may concern, this letter is to formally notify you of the rescue.’ Explain what is wrong with this opening and suggest a better one.
items.answer: It is cold and impersonal; a thank-you letter should be warm and sincere. Better: ‘Dear Mr Ndlovu, I will never forget the moment your torch found us in the cloud.’
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: identifies the problem of form/register/voice; 1 mark: improved opening that suits the role and audience.

items.stem: Task: “Imagine you are the student who wrote the report. You give a speech in a Year 10 assembly to persuade students to waste less food.” These sentences come from the report ‘Canteen Food Waste Report’: “The largest single source of waste was rice, which accounted for almost a third of the total, followed by cooked vegetables. … Finally, uneaten food that is safe to use should be offered to the local food bank, with which the school already has links.” Explain how you would use each detail in your response, developing it from the point of view of the student who wrote the report.
items.answer: Rice as the biggest waste: ask for smaller portions if you will not finish. The food bank recommendation: waste could feed local families instead.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per detail identified and 1 mark per detail developed in role (max 4): rice as the biggest waste → ask for smaller portions if you will not finish; the food bank recommendation → waste could feed local families instead.

items.stem: Read the travel writing ‘Crossing the Salt Flats’: “Nothing prepares you for the whiteness. We left the last village at sunrise, and within twenty minutes the land had flattened into a blinding plain of salt that stretched to every horizon. Our driver, Luis, wore two pairs of sunglasses at once and still squinted. In the rainy season, he told us, a thin layer of water turns the flats into the world’s largest mirror, and the sky appears both above and below you. We had come in the dry season, so instead the ground was cracked into hexagons, each one rimmed with a crust of salt as neat as icing on a cake. At noon Luis stopped the jeep and switched off the engine. The silence was so complete that I could hear the blood moving in my ears. There were no birds, no insects, no wind — only an enormous, humming emptiness. I had travelled a long way to see a famous view. I had not expected to be moved by the absence of one.” Imagine you are Luis, the driver. You write an entry for a travel guidebook advising visitors to the salt flats. In your guide, you should write about: the best time of year to visit and why; what visitors will see and experience; how to stay safe and comfortable. Base your answer on what you have read, but be careful to use your own words. Write about 250–300 words.
items.answer: Model opening: Visitors ask me every week: when should I come? My answer depends on what you want to see. Come in the rainy season and you will drive across the sky itself… The response then develops: the rainy-season mirror (visit in the rainy season for reflections, dry season for hexagons); the glare (bring strong sunglasses and sun protection); the dry-season ground (a different but equally striking sight); the silence at noon (many visitors are moved by the stillness; switch off engines and listen).
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10 (extended response in role (guide)): Reading 5 marks, Writing 5 marks. Reading – top band (5): ideas from the passage are thoroughly used, developed and extended with convincing inferences; all three bullets addressed; a consistent, convincing voice; middle band (3–4): relevant ideas with some development or selection; lower band (1–2): few relevant ideas, often lifted or repeated. Writing – top band (5): fluent, well organised, own words, register and form fully suited to the task; middle band (3–4): clear and mostly accurate, some own words; lower band (1–2): lifted phrases, weak organisation or frequent errors. Indicative content: The rainy-season mirror → visit in the rainy season for reflections, dry season for hexagons. The glare → bring strong sunglasses and sun protection. The dry-season ground → a different but equally striking sight. The silence at noon → many visitors are moved by the stillness; switch off engines and listen. Form: practical advice organised clearly for visitors; second-person address and an informative, enthusiastic tone.

items.stem: Read the magazine article ‘The Return of the Urban Beekeeper’: “On the flat roof of a bank in central Toronto, eighty thousand bees are hard at work. Their keeper, Grace Lin, climbs a fire escape every Thursday to check the six hives, which produce around 150 jars of honey a year. ‘People expect city honey to taste of exhaust fumes,’ she laughs. ‘In fact, it’s often better than country honey.’ The reason is variety. While farmland bees may feed on a single crop for weeks, city bees forage in parks, gardens, balconies and roadside verges, collecting nectar from hundreds of different plants. Urban beekeeping has boomed over the past decade, but not all experts are delighted. Some ecologists warn that too many honeybee hives in a small area can leave too little food for wild bees, which are often more important pollinators. Lin agrees that numbers must be managed. She now spends as much time planting wildflowers on rooftops as she does tending her hives. ‘A beehive without flowers,’ she says, ‘is just a box of hungry insects.’” Imagine you are Grace Lin. You give a talk to residents encouraging them to plant wildflowers on balconies and rooftops. In your speech, you should write about: what your bees do in the city; the problem experts have warned about; how residents can help. Base your answer on what you have read, but be careful to use your own words. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model opening: Good evening. Above your heads, on the roof of the bank on King Street, eighty thousand of my bees are asleep. Tomorrow they will be looking for breakfast — and I need your help to feed them… The response then develops: the rooftop hives (the city is already home to many bees); bees forage widely (every balcony counts as a food source); wild bees at risk (more flowers support both wild and honeybees); her own planting (practical steps and an example to follow).
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 12 (extended response in role (speech)): Reading 6 marks, Writing 6 marks. Reading – top band (5–6): ideas from the passage are thoroughly used, developed and extended with convincing inferences; all three bullets addressed; a consistent, convincing voice; middle band (3–4): relevant ideas with some development or selection; lower band (1–2): few relevant ideas, often lifted or repeated. Writing – top band (5–6): fluent, well organised, own words, register and form fully suited to the task; middle band (3–4): clear and mostly accurate, some own words; lower band (1–2): lifted phrases, weak organisation or frequent errors. Indicative content: The rooftop hives → the city is already home to many bees. Bees forage widely → every balcony counts as a food source. Wild bees at risk → more flowers support both wild and honeybees. Her own planting → practical steps and an example to follow. Form: direct address to the listeners, e.g. “Good evening, everyone”; rhetorical devices such as questions, repetition and a call to action.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Developed ideas should always be (b) Which assessment objective is most clearly rewarded when you extend and develop ideas from a text?
items.answer: (a) consistent with the evidence in the passage (b) R3

items.stem: Writing as Mum, develop this detail from the short story ‘The Power Cut’ into two or three sentences that infer thoughts, feelings or consequences: ‘Then my little sister laughed, a high nervous sound, and Dad’s chair scraped back as he went to find the torch he swore was in the drawer by the sink.’
items.answer: Detail: Dad searching for the torch. Developed in role: affectionate amusement at his confidence.

items.stem: Task based on the short story ‘Stranded’: “Imagine you are Aiko. After the storm you write a letter to the warden of the mountain hut. In your letter, you should write about: what happened on the walk and during the storm; how you and Kenji kept safe; what advice the hut should give other walkers.” Relevant lines: “By three o’clock the sky over the ridge had turned the colour of a bruise. Kenji and his sister had been walking since dawn, and the hut they were aiming for was still two hours away. … ‘We go back,’ Aiko shouted, ‘to the overhang!’ … They sat shoulder to shoulder, shaking, and listened to the mountain roar.” (a) Identify two details from the lines that you could use in your response, and state which bullet point each would support. (b) Explain why developed ideas are rewarded more highly than repeated ones.
items.answer: (a) Sheltering together; walking since dawn and still two hours from the hut (each linked to a suitable bullet). (b) R3 rewards developing and evaluating ideas; repetition only shows basic understanding (R1).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per relevant detail linked to a bullet [2] (b) link to R3 [2]

items.stem: A student writing for school governors wrote: ‘Basically, homework is doing everyone’s heads in.’ Rewrite it in an appropriate register and explain your choices.
items.answer: ‘Homework is causing considerable stress for many students and their families.’ – formal vocabulary (‘considerable’) and no idiom.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: meaning kept in an appropriate formal register; 1 mark: explanation of a specific change (e.g. formal vocabulary (‘considerable’) and no idiom).

items.answer: ‘Let’s be honest: we all spend way too long on our phones.’ – inclusive ‘we’, conversational ‘way too long’.

items.stem: What is the writer’s attitude in the letter to a newspaper ‘Protect Our Night Sky’? Explain with reference to: ‘A simple solution exists: motion-sensor lighting, which switches on only when someone is present.’
items.answer: The writer is concerned and firm, but polite and reasonable. The words ‘A simple solution exists’ show this (constructive rather than just critical).
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: attitude (concerned and firm, but polite and reasonable); 1 mark: explanation of how the quotation shows it (constructive rather than just critical).

items.stem: Read this extract from the news article ‘Flood Recovery in the River District’: “Three months after the River Kali burst its banks, recovery in the River District is uneven. Of the 1,400 homes flooded, around 900 have been repaired and reoccupied. … Local businesses have been hit hard.” Explain how the writer uses a fact to support their viewpoint.
items.answer: Of the 1,400 homes flooded, around 900 have been repaired gives verifiable support, making the writer’s view seem reasonable and evidence-based.
items.markingKey: fact linked to view [2]
